title: I deposted $25,000 into Public, connected it via MCP to Claude, and let it trade. I'm up over $3,000
author: NextgenAITrading
selftext:
I created the Public Portfolio Challenge, an open challenge where I watch AI agents build algorithmic trading strategies to manage over $25,000.  

So far, I'm destroying the market. 

The book trades options on high-momentum stocks in my personal watchlist. I trained it using walk forward optimization, and deployed it to Public via OAuth.with my platform. 

You can see the exact rules, the trading strategies, and my updates for free. I even have an open-source GitHub repo where you can download skills to follow along in Claude Code or Codex.

Happy to answer any questions below!

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Publishing the rules and the live portfolio is the right level of transparency. A 12.7% gain on options of high-momentum stocks in a rising market can come mostly from leverage and exposure, so I'd show the result next to the same watchlist held in shares and SPY over the same dates, plus max drawdown and the number of trades. Since the watchlist is personal, I'd also ask how it was chosen: a list picked after those stocks moved is itself a form of look-ahead, even with walk-forward optimization on the rest. Earnings and macro dates drive options P&L, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for earnings and macro releases) is one source for splitting results around them.

comments.author: Training_Clerk_2383
comments.body: up $3,000 on $25,000 is roughly 12%, but over what time period, and how much of that is realized? With options on high-momentum names, the comparison gets messy unless we can see the exposure and drawdowns. A short run during a rally can look incredible before one reversal eats the gains. I'm interested in the walk-forward setup. Did you lock the watchlist before each test window, or choose it using stocks you currently follow? That could introduce selection bias even if the parameter fitting itself was clean. Also, were fills modeled at executable prices with commissions, or at the midpoint? The Claude connection raises a separate question: is it generating strategies and handing orders to a deterministic execution layer, or deciding what to buy each time it reads new information? Those would need different failure tests. I'd want to know what happens if the broker request times out after an order actually fills. Could you share the live start date and worst peak-to-trough drawdown alongside the returns? The repo sounds useful, especially if it includes rejected orders and losing trades rather than only the current strategy. That would make the challenge much easier to evaluate

replies.author: Mobile-Growth2053
replies.body: That timeout question deserves its own test. A successful backtest won't catch an agent submitting the same order twice because the first response never arrived. I'd look for broker-supported client order IDs and a reconciliation step before retries. OAuth also doesn't tell us what permissions were granted or whether position limits are enforced outside Claude

replies.author: Quick-Fisherman-2973
replies.body: The permissions point is what I'd like to understand before trying any financial mcp tool. If Claude can change the limits that are supposed to constrain Claude, those limits don't give me much comfort. I'd want the execution service to reject an oversized order regardless of what the conversation says. Does that approach translate to crypto wallets, or are there different mcp tools for that? I'm asking about a separate small test wallet, not moving this options strategy onto a chain. Checking a balance through chat seems straightforward; authorizing a token swap seems like a different level of access. Would something built around MetaMask or Coinbase AgentKit keep signing credentials out of the model context? And how would you check whether a timed-out swap was submitted before letting the agent try again?

replies.author: Beautiful_Fall_1198
replies.body: Your separate test wallet would let you check the permissions without involving an account of that size. I’d begin in read-only mode, then enable a small transfer and deliberately request an amount above the cap. The expected result is a rejection from the wallet service. I’d repeat the test with an address outside the approved list. For tooling, I’d compare MetaMask’s manual review workflow with Coinbase AgentKit and Iron. I’d inspect the signing path and policy controls for each configuration, including whether the connected agent can modify them. Keeping signing credentials out of the conversation is useful, but it doesn’t settle what the agent is allowed to execute. For swaps, I’d record the operation identifier before proceeding. If the response times out, use that identifier and any available transaction hash to establish what happened on the correct network. A missing chat response isn’t enough reason to submit again. I’d test repeated payments below the limit as well, and leave enough native currency for fees. That would give you evidence about spending controls and recovery behavior. Whether the original stock strategy has an edge remains a separate question
